h1: Electric press brakes — servo ball-screw drive, 3 to 176 US tons
intro: An electric press brake has no hydraulic system at all: servo motors drive the ram through timing belts and ball screws, so there is no oil to heat, no pump idling between bends, no valves to drift and no warm-up — the ram repeats to ± 0.01 mm from the first part, bends at any programmed speed up to 30 mm/s and the machine draws power only while it moves. NovoTech sells its own value-line electric press brakes in Canada: ten models from 11 US tons × 20″ to 176 US tons × 10.5 ft with a Delem DA-53T control and X-R servo back gauge, and three bench-size 3, 6 and 12 ton machines for electronics and small-parts work. For the Turkish-built DDM servo-electric brakes to 220 tons see the Dener press brake page. Installed and supported from Mississauga, ON, with a CSA-approved panel.

groups.title: Electric servo press brakes
groups.lead: Ball-screw servo drive from 3 to 176 US tons — the clean, quiet, accurate brake for sheet work.

faq.a: Electric wins on accuracy, speed on thin material, energy and cleanliness: ± 0.01 mm repeatability from the first part, bending speeds to 30 mm/s instead of 10, about 70 % less power, no oil, no cooler, no noise between bends. Hydraulic wins on price per ton above about 150 tons and on thick plate, where the full tonnage is needed over the whole stroke. For a shop bending 16 ga to 1/4″ sheet all day — enclosures, brackets, HVAC, electrical — the electric brake is usually the better buy; for 3/8″ and 1/2″ plate, buy the hydraulic CNC.

faq.q: How does the ball-screw drive work?
faq.a: Two servo motors (three on the 160 t) on top of the frame drive lead ball screws through timing belts; the screws move the ram, and magnetic scales on each side feed the position back to the control so the two sides stay in step to 0.01 mm. Because the screws hold position without power, the ram can dwell at the bottom for coining or hemming with no energy drawn. The screws are preloaded and lubricated automatically; there is nothing to bleed or change.

faq.q: What about the small 3 – 13 ton machines?
faq.a: They are the same drive in a bench-height cabinet: 8, 16 and 24″ bending lengths, 4.7″ stroke, 16.5″ daylight, a touchscreen control with X and R back gauge axes and quick-change tooling, 28 – 33″ square on the floor and plugged into a wall outlet. They are bought for electronics enclosures, instrument panels, brackets and prototypes — anywhere a 100-ton machine is overkill and a hand brake is not accurate enough.

The Delem DA-53T touchscreen control is standard, with DA-66S and DA-69S 3D controls and the ESA S875 as options; the machines program in inches or millimetres and import DXF. Tooling is European-style with mechanical quick clamps and a 2-V die as standard, Wila hydraulic clamping as an option; NovoTech stocks Eurostamp punches and dies in Canada.

faq.q: Can the electric brake be automated?
faq.a: Yes — the 40 and 50 ton machines are sold as complete robot bending cells with an Estun robot, gripper, loading table and unloading stack, and every model has the robot interface. An electric brake is the natural machine for a cell: the ram position is deterministic, so the robot timing never drifts.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models with a small enough motor. Manual machines have no electrics.
